sections.b: Paul's comparison of Adam and Christ is the New Testament's central text on how sin and death spread. "sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death passed to all people, because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). The Greek eph' ho pantes hemarton was read in Latin as "in whom all sinned," which shaped Augustine's teaching of inherited guilt; most modern commentators take the Greek as "because," and the Eastern churches speak of inherited death and a bent toward sin without guilt (ancestral sin). Pelagius read it of imitation. Paul adds that the gift in Christ is larger than the damage (5:15-17), and that Adam is "a figure of the one who was coming" (5:14). The note at 5:12 and the card on this page give each church's reading.

sections.h: Romans 7 and 8: sin as a power, creation under futility
sections.b: Paul speaks of sin as a ruler that "found its opening in the commandment" and tricked "me," an echo of Eve and the snake (Romans 7:8-11; Genesis 3:13). In Romans 8:19-22 the whole creation was "subjected to futility" and groans, waiting for freedom: the Genesis curse seen from the side of the world, not only of humans.

common: Paul sets Adam's one act against Christ's one act in Romans 5:12-21 and says the gift is greater than the trespass.
uncommon: Some scholars find Adam in the first-person "I" of Romans 7:7-13, and Israel at Sinai in the same verses.

sections.b: Paul names Adam only in Romans 5:14 ("death ruled from Adam until Moses"), where he calls him "a figure of the one who was coming," but he writes of "one man" through 5:12-19, a man whose single act affected all. The text takes no side on whether Genesis 2-3 is history, parable or both; readers have taken Adam as the first individual, as a figure of every person ("each of us is our own Adam," 2 Baruch 54:19, a Jewish book written about AD 100), or as the head of a first human family. Many see Adam and Eve echoed in the "I" of Romans 7:7-13, where the commandment, the tricking by sin and death repeat Genesis 2-3.

sections.h: Romans 5-8: what follows from being justified
sections.b: After the argument of chapters 1-4, Paul traces the results: peace with God (5:1), salvation from the coming anger (5:9), life instead of condemnation (5:16-18), freedom from sin (6:7, where the same Greek verb is translated "freed"), and no condemnation (8:1, 33-34). The "justified" of 8:30 is the center of the chain between "called" and "glorified." Chapter 5 sets "justification of life" against Adam's "condemnation" (5:18). The Reformation churches stress that this is a declaration of right standing; Catholic and Orthodox writers stress the inner renewal that goes with it.
sections.refs: Romans 5:1; Romans 5:9; Romans 5:16-19; Romans 6:7; Romans 8:1; Romans 8:30; Romans 8:33-34

sections.b: Paul says grace "overflowed" where sin multiplied (5:20), that it rules through righteousness to eternal life (5:21), and that believers are "under grace" not under law (6:14-15). He answers the objection "shall we sin so that grace may multiply?" with "By no means!" (6:1-2). The last line of chapter 6 states it in a single contrast: sin pays wages, but God gives a gift (6:23).

"We have been justified by faith," and so we have peace with God and are led by faith into grace (Romans 5:1-2). Faith is the way the gift is received. Hope is its companion: "in hope we were saved," and a hope that is seen is no hope, so believers wait for what they do not yet see with endurance (Romans 8:24-25).

Paul speaks of "the anger" (he orge) from which the justified are saved (Romans 5:9), as he did in 1:18 and 2:5. He does not say whether it is a person's final judgment, the working out of sin's results, or both. Chapter 8:7 describes the mind of the flesh as hostile to God, and 5:10 says that we were enemies and were reconciled. The anger is real; so is the reconciliation.

Paul writes to people he has not yet met and assumes that they were all baptized: "those of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death" (Romans 6:3). He uses the rite as the picture of dying to sin and rising to a new life: "we were buried with him" so that "we also might walk in a life that is new" (6:4). The churches differ on how baptism works (a sacrament that gives new life; a sign and seal; an act of the believer) and on how it is given (by immersion, by pouring, to infants or to believers). The card at Romans 6 sets them side by side.

The Spirit pours God's love into hearts (Romans 5:5), makes a new way of serving possible (7:6), sets believers free from the law of sin and death (8:2), lives in them (8:9-11), leads them (8:14), cries "Abba, Father!" in them (8:15), joins their spirit in testifying that they are children (8:16), is the firstfruits of the coming redemption (8:23) and pleads for them with groans too deep for words (8:26-27). Chapter 8 mentions the Spirit nearly twenty times, more than any other chapter in Paul's letters. In 8:9-11 "the Spirit of God," "the Spirit of Christ" and "Christ in you" are used interchangeably.

Paul ties believers to Christ's resurrection in two ways: they walk in new life now (6:4), and God "will also bring your mortal bodies to life" by his Spirit (8:11). The hope is for the body, not release from it: "the redemption of our bodies" (8:23). The background in Ezekiel 37, where the Spirit raises dry bones, is likely.

Paul says the law "slipped in so that the trespass would multiply" (5:20), that believers are "not under law" (6:14), that they were put to death in relation to the law (7:4) and released from it (7:6). Then he defends it: it is not sin (7:7), it is "holy, righteous and good" (7:12), "spiritual" (7:14), and "God's law" even for the hostile mind (8:7). What the law could not do, because of the flesh, God did in his Son, so that "what the law rightly requires" would be fulfilled in believers (8:3-4). Readers differ on whether "law" is always the Torah (Dunn, Wright) or sometimes a principle (older commentators), and whether the "I" of chapter 7 is Israel under Moses.

sections.h: The tenth word as the test case (Romans 7:7)
sections.b: Paul quotes the last of the Ten Words ("You must not crave") to show how the law works. It is the one commandment that forbids a desire and not an act, so it shows that sin is in the heart. Other Jewish writers of his time used it the same way (4 Maccabees 2:5-6; Philo, On the Decalogue 142-153).

sections.h: God sent his Son 'as a sin offering' (Romans 8:3)
sections.b: The Greek peri hamartias ("about sin") is the Greek Old Testament's usual phrase for the sin offering of Leviticus 4-5 and 16. Paul uses it in Romans 8:3 for the sending of the Son, who "condemned sin in the flesh." Many commentators read it as a sin offering; others as "to deal with sin." Hebrews 10:6-8 uses the same phrase for the offering.
Paul says believers are justified "by his blood" and so will be saved from God's anger (Romans 5:9). Blood stands for a life given, as in Leviticus 17:11 and the Passover. See also Romans 3:25.

Trouble builds endurance, tested character and hope (Romans 5:3-5); believers are heirs "as long as we suffer with him" (8:17); the present sufferings do not weigh against the coming glory (8:18); and none of hardship, famine, danger or the sword can separate us from Christ's love (8:35-39). Paul quotes Psalm 44:22, a psalm of innocent suffering, for the way of God's people (8:36).

Paul says the creation "stands on tiptoe" waiting for God's children to be revealed, was "subjected to futility" in hope, and will "be set free from slavery to decay." The whole creation "groans as one and is in labor as one" with believers, who have the Spirit as the firstfruits. The picture is of a new creation that includes the natural world, in line with Isaiah 65:17 and Revelation 21:1.

Paul's picture of the creation as subjected to futility and groaning in labor is a New Testament commentary on the curse of Genesis 3:17-19. Modern readers have used it in discussions of care for creation (for example Pope Francis in Laudato Si', 2015); others warn that Paul's hope is for a transformed world, not for managing the present one.

Romans 8:29-30 is the passage on which most Christian teaching on predestination rests: "Those he knew beforehand, he also decided beforehand would be formed to match the image of his Son ... He called the ones he decided beforehand. He justified the ones he called. And he glorified the ones he justified." The goal is the image of the Son, and the people are called "God's chosen" (8:33), Israel's title. The Reformed read the chain as an unbroken line from free choice to glory; Arminians and Wesleyans read "foreknew" as foreseeing faith; Catholics, Lutherans and Orthodox have their own accounts. The card at 8:29-30 sets them side by side. Chapter 9 takes the theme further.

Romans 8:31-39 is the closing argument of the first eight chapters: God is for us, God gave his Son, God justifies, Christ pleads, and nothing in all creation "will have power to separate us from God's love, the love that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (8:39). The churches ask whether this means that a believer cannot lose salvation, or that no outside power can take it. The card on this page gives the answers of the Reformed, Baptists, Methodists, Lutherans, Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Pentecostals.

sections.h: Heirs, glorified, formed to match the Son (Romans 8:17, 29-30)
sections.b: The Eastern churches find the root of theosis in Romans 8:17 (heirs "sharing the inheritance with Christ" and "glorified with him") and 8:29-30 ("formed to match the image of his Son ... he glorified the ones he justified"). The Catholic Catechism quotes Athanasius: the Son of God became man "that we might become God" (460). Western Protestants speak of conformity to Christ and sanctification.

Paul says that those God chose are "formed to match the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29). Christ is the true image (Colossians 1:15), and humans, made in the image of God in Genesis 1:26-27, are restored by being made like him. The Adam theme of Romans 5-8 returns.

Believers have "the Spirit as the firstfruits," a first installment of the harvest, and yet wait for the redemption of their bodies. As with the Feast of Weeks (Leviticus 23:15-21), the first sheaf promises the rest.

sections.h: Slaves of sin, slaves of righteousness (Romans 6:15-23)
sections.b: Paul uses the Roman slave market for his picture: you are the slave of whomever you obey, either of sin, which ends in death, or of obedience, which ends in righteousness (6:16). He says he speaks "in human terms" (6:19). He does not comment on the institution; later readers have both used and argued against the passage in debates on slavery. The wages image is from the army: sin pays wages, and the wages are death (6:23).
The Greek mataiotes is the Septuagint's word for Hebrew hevel, the "vapor" of Ecclesiastes. Paul says the creation was "subjected to futility" by God's choice, in hope.

sections.h: The Spirit and Christ plead for us (Romans 8:26-27, 34)
sections.b: The Spirit "pleads for us, with groanings that words cannot say" (8:26), and Christ at God's right hand "pleads for us" (8:34). The two ideas answer the problem of prayer: we do not know what to pray for, and we need someone to speak for us.

The "glory of God" which all lack (3:23) becomes in Romans 5-8 the hope of believers: they boast "in the hope of God's glory" (5:2), will be "glorified with him" (8:17), and enter "the freedom of the glory of God's children" (8:21). By 8:30 it is spoken of as done.

The Spirit cries "Abba, Father!" in believers (8:15). The popular idea that abba means "Daddy" was given up after James Barr's article of 1988. In 8:26 the Spirit pleads with groanings that words cannot say; some read them as tongues, most as wordless prayer.

Paul lists "angels," "rulers" and "powers" among the things that cannot separate believers from God's love. They are most often read as spiritual beings, whether loyal or hostile; see also Ephesians 1:21 and Colossians 2:15.

sections.h: 'He did not hold back his own Son' (Romans 8:32)
sections.b: Paul's wording echoes God's words to Abraham at the binding of Isaac: "you have not held back your son, your only one" (Genesis 22:12). God does what Abraham was spared from doing. Jewish tradition read the binding as a source of merit and atonement.

sections.h: Adam as a figure of Christ (Romans 5:14)
sections.b: Paul calls Adam "a figure of the one who was coming" (Romans 5:14). The Greek typos is the mark of a stamp, a pattern; the likeness is by contrast as well as by resemblance.

sections.h: Father, Son and Spirit in Romans 8:9-11
sections.b: In Romans 8:9-11 Paul moves between "the Spirit of God," "the Spirit of Christ," "Christ in you" and the Father who raised Jesus. Later theology took it as part of the base for the doctrine of the Trinity and the debate about the Spirit's procession.
The verse is often read as a promise that every event is good. In Paul the "good" is the goal of 8:29, being formed to match the image of the Son. Some early manuscripts make God the subject.
Paul speaks of "his own Son" (8:3, 32), a phrase stronger than the "sons" and "children" of 8:14-17: the Son is sent and given, and believers become children by adoption.

God decided beforehand that believers would be formed like his Son, "so that his Son would be the firstborn among many brothers" (8:29). The title, from Psalm 89:27, makes Christ the elder brother of a large family.

"What I want to do, I do not do. What I hate, that is what I do" (7:15). The passage has been central to teaching on the will: Augustine read it as evidence of the will bound by sin; the Greek fathers read it of life before grace; Wesley as the person under conviction; Luther in The Bondage of the Will argued from Paul's view that the will is not free to choose good by its own power. Greek and Roman writers (Euripides, Ovid, Epictetus) described a similar split between knowing and doing.

The first-person "I" of Romans 7 has been read as Paul's own experience of sin, of the law, or of a speech in character. Krister Stendahl argued in 1963 that the West had read its own "introspective conscience" into Paul, who elsewhere says he was blameless under the law (Philippians 3:6).

Paul says believers "received the Spirit of adoption as children" (Romans 8:15), and still "wait for adoption as children, the redemption of our bodies" (8:23). The same word names a gift of Israel (9:4). The note at 8:15 sets out the Roman law behind the word, and the note at 8:14 explains why the Plain says "children" where the Greek has "sons."
